newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy economy to see only slight growth in 97 - BOI.
newsitem.headline: Italy economy to see only slight growth in 97 - BOI.

text.p: Italy's economy may revive a little in 1997 but growth is likely to be subdued as the government tightens the fiscal screws in a race to prepare for European currency union, the central bank said on Friday.
"The rate of growth of the Italian economy in 1997 could prove to be slightly higher than that in 1996," said the semi-annual report.
The economy teetered on the edge of recession last year, growing by just 0.8 percent, according to official estimates.

But efforts by Italy's European Union partners -- particularly Germany -- to meet qualifying criteria for joining European economic and monetary union (EMU) through public spending cuts could hit consumption in Italy's key export markets.

"The European countries for whom EMU participation is on the cards are simultaneously carrying out tough measures of fiscal restructuring. This could lead to a weakening in the revival of consumption and investment started in the second half of 1996," said the Bank of Italy in a six-monthly report.
With Italy's export performance already showing signs of flagging, economic revival would depend on consumption by households picking up in the course of the year.
"In the light of the limited contribution expected from exports, such a prospect is subordinated to an acceleration during the year of consumption by families," the report added.
The central bank was more optimistic about the prospects for keeping inflation in check despite a surge in wage settlements in recent negotiations between trade unions and employers.

"The renewal of the main national collective contracts and company agreements concluded until now have determined for the coming months significant increases in the cost of labour," it said. "The scale of these increases is however compatible with an inflation rate of below an average of three percent."
The government hopes to keep consumer price inflation at no higher than an average of 2.5 percent this year, down from a 1996 average of 3.9 percent.
Monetary policy would be aimed at achieving a lasting fall in inflation, currently running at a year-on-year rate of 2.6 percent.
"The orientation of monetary policy remains targeted at making the fall in inflation durable, favouring an improvement in expectations and countering any emergence of risk factors."
Keeping the lira stable on foreign exchange markets would also play a key part in ensuring that inflation targets were met.

The central bank also sent a clear signal to the government that more fiscal belt-tightening was needed to narrow the ratio of the public sector deficit to gross domestic product to three percent in 1997 -- a key criterion for EMU membership.
Unless a supplementary budget was adopted, the ratio was likely to fall by no more than three percentage points in 1997 from 6.8 percent in 1996, the central bank said.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government passed a tough 62.5 trillion lira ($37 billion) 1997 budget at the end of last year as part of a campaign to qualify as a founding member of EMU, planned for launch in 1999.
But it is widely accepted that the budget did not do enough to put Italy's finances in order.
"In the absence of further measures, the reduction of the ratio, compared to the 1996 level, may not surpass three percentage points," the central bank said.
The government is now expected to introduce a supplementary budget in the coming weeks which would attempt to slice a further 14-15 trillion lire off the 1997 budget deficit.
